🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
PyTorch Process Group Shrink API
Authors: @brchang24 @spotluri @bosilca
Summary
This document outlines proposed API changes to improve fault tolerance and flexibility in PyTorch Process Groups.
Motivation
Fault Tolerance support
The API is designed to enhance fault tolerance capabilities in PyTorch by enabling exclusion of faulty ranks.
With the new API, malfunctioning participants should be excluded to avoid hangings, as their reliability can't be guaranteed. This API is not limited to hard faults (where processes disappear due to hardware failures) but allows the application to mold the execution environment as needed (for correctness or performance reasons).
Performance
The existing abort + init method entails a fixed cost for full initialization, as illustrated in the chart below with rank shrink as an example.

We also explored alternatives like split, but that approach requires the participation of all ranks, including malfunctioning ones, to form a new group.
So, both above factors must be considered when designing the API.
Proposed API changes
To address these concerns above, we are proposing the following API changes:
New API: shrink_group()
shrink_group(ranks_to_exclude: List[int],
            Pg: Optional[ProcessGroup] = None,
            shrink_flags : int = NCCL_SHRINK_DEFAULT)

Shrink an existing distributed group. Only group members of the updated ProcessGroup need to enter this function. The excluded ranks do not need to call this function. The scope of this call is therefore collective across the processes that belong to the shrunk distributed group.

Args:
ranks_exclude (list[int]):  List of group ranks to be excluded in the updated ProcessGroup. This list must be consistent across all participating processes.
pg (ProcessGroup, optional): The process group to work on, If None, the default process group will be used.
shrink_flags (int): NCCL_SHRINK_DEFAULT (default)
                    NCCL_SHRINK_ABORT (attempt to terminate ongoing operations in the parent communicator before shrinking. 
Implementation
PyTorch should directly use the shrink functionality if supported by the backend.
Use Cases
Rank Shrink
When one rank is detected defective and needs to be excluded, the new shrink_group() can be invoked as the below example:
Example
remove rank 2
shrink_group([2], pg)

In the example above, only the original rank 0, 1, and 3 need to invoke shrink_group(), not rank 2 to avoid potential hang. After the shrink, the original rank 2 is excluded, so, the original rank 3 will be shifted down to become rank 2 in the updated group, if no parameter key is passed in.
Errors could be reported by the backend or PyTorch. However, it is up to the upper layer to decide whether to exclude a rank from the group.
Ideally, the defective ranks should be excluded from all associated groups. However, it appears to be enforcing a policy on PyTorch. This design suggests delegating the decision to exclude ranks from a group or completely dissolve the group to the Upper Layer (UL). Meanwhile, PyTorch should verify that no subgroups use the rank before it is removed from the default group.
Things to Consider
Group Rank recalculation
Shrink can lead to changes in the group's rank order. It will apply the default method to recalculate group ranks as detailed below.
When shrinking, ranks will be shifted to close any gaps left by excluded ranks.
Metrics
What are the main metrics to measure the value of this feature?


When one node/rank goes down completely
To compare with the existing solution.


Performance comparison with the existing solutions


Shrink


Drawbacks
Are there any reasons why we should not do this? Here we aim to evaluate risk and check ourselves.
Please consider:

Is it a breaking change?
This change should be backward compatible.
Impact on UX
No
implementation cost, both in terms of code size and complexity
The assumption is that the pytorch cost should not be high, but the backend support cost might be high, especially for backends that do not have already support for fault management.
integration of this feature with other existing and planned features
PyTorch layer needs to integrate with the backend when it has the support.

Alternatives
What other designs have been considered? What is the impact of not doing this?
Can be implemented using abort+init method.
Need full init method which potentially requires broadcast for the NCCL bootstrap.
Prior Art
Discuss prior art (both good and bad) in relation to this proposal:

Does this feature exist in other libraries? What experience has their community had?
MPI has similar concepts with steady adoption in highly scalable HPC applications and runtimes.
What lessons can be learned from other implementations of this feature?
Such as NCCL shrink API
Published papers or great posts that discuss this
n/a

How we teach this


There are some new concepts introduced after this RFC


exclude ranks


the PyTorch documentation needs to include the API changes
shrink_group()
This is a new API and should be added.


How should this feature be taught to existing PyTorch users
Including a section with examples would be ideal to demonstrate how shrink use cases function with the proposed new API changes.


Unresolved questions


What parts of the design do you expect to resolve through the RFC process before this gets merged?
No


What parts of the design do you expect to resolve through the implementation of this feature before stabilization?
No


What related issues do you consider out of scope for this RFC that could be addressed in the future independently of the solution that comes out of this RFC?
No

🐛 Describe the bug
I'm not sure if this is considered an issue by the torch team, since _int_mm and _scaled_mm are not part of a stable and documented API. If not, feel free to close it.
_scaled_mm raises an error if the rhs matrix is row-major. _int_mm does not, but it is very slow in benchmarks. Presumably, it does a transparent rhs.T.contiguous().T before applying the mm.
both column-major and row-major rhs matrices are common use cases, because your weights matrix in a Linear layer is transposed for your forward pass and not transposed for your backward. So either one of those will be row-major, no matter how you store it.
Attached you can find a Triton kernel that we are using instead for this case. It's not as optimized as torch kernels, but due to its strided access to the matrix it is much faster than convert the matrix to column-major first.
triton_mm_8bit(3).py

import torch

torch.manual_seed(238)

def fuzzed_program(arg_0, sentinel):
    var_node_2 = torch.full((), 1, dtype=torch.int16) # size=(), stride=(), dtype=int16, device=cuda
    var_node_3 = arg_0 # size=(), stride=(), dtype=int16, device=cuda
    var_node_1 = torch.add(var_node_2, var_node_3) # size=(), stride=(), dtype=int16, device=cuda
    var_node_5 = torch.full((1,), 3, dtype=torch.int16) # size=(1,), stride=(1,), dtype=int16, device=cuda
    var_node_4 = torch.squeeze(var_node_5) # size=(), stride=(), dtype=int16, device=cuda
    var_node_0 = torch.div(var_node_1, var_node_4) # size=(), stride=(), dtype=int16, device=cuda
    # Ensure gradient computation by multiplying with sentinel and taking real part
    result = var_node_0 * sentinel
    if result.is_complex():
        result = result.real
    return result

# Sentinel tensor to ensure gradient computation

🐛 Describe the bug
Goal of my experiment was to build an ONNX QDQ equivalent in PyTorch, meaning that on each tensor in the graph quantize-dequantize operation is applied. I figured that using TorchDispatchMode would be an elegant solution as it allows to intercept elementary functions and apply quantization operation on its arguments and outputs.
However, the issue I came across is that I'm not able to export such model to ONNX with proper QuantizeLinear and DequantizeLinear nodes.
Code to reproduce:
from torch.utils._python_dispatch import TorchDispatchMode
import torch.onnx
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def quantize_linear_onnx(x, scale, zp):
    return torch.onnx.ops.symbolic(
                        "QuantizeLinear",
                        (x, scale, zp),
                        attrs = {},
                        dtype = zp.dtype,
                        shape = x.shape
                    )
def dequantize_linear_onnx(x, scale, zp):
    return torch.onnx.ops.symbolic(
                        "DequantizeLinear",
                        (x, scale, zp),
                        attrs = {},
                        dtype = scale.dtype,
                        shape = x.shape
                    )
def qdq_onnx(x, scale, zp):
    q = quantize_linear_onnx(x, scale, zp)
    dq = dequantize_linear_onnx(q, scale, zp)
    return dq

class Quantizer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, scale, zero_point):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer('scale', scale)
        self.register_buffer('zero_point', zero_point)

    def forward(self, x):
        return qdq_onnx(x, self.scale, self.zero_point)

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.lin1 = nn.Linear(hidden, hidden, bias=False)
        self.lin2 = nn.Linear(hidden, hidden, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        residual = x
        y = self.lin1(x)          # op set 1
        y = torch.relu(y)         # op set 2
        y = self.lin2(y)          # op set 3
        return y + residual       # op set 4 (add)


class ToyModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden: int = 16, num_blocks: int = 2):
        super().__init__()
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([Block(hidden) for _ in range(num_blocks)])
        self.proj = nn.Linear(hidden, hidden, bias=False)

    def forward(self, a: torch.Tensor, b: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = a + b                 # top-level add (index in root module)
        for blk in self.blocks:
            x = blk(x)
        x = self.proj(x)          # linear at root
        return x.mean(dim=-1)     # reduction

class QuantManager:
    def __init__(self, model: nn.Module):
        self.model = model
        self.dispatch_ctx = None
        scale = torch.tensor(0.1, dtype=torch.float32)
        zero_point = torch.tensor(128, dtype=torch.uint8)

        quantizer = Quantizer(scale, zero_point)
        self.model.register_module("quantizer", quantizer)

    def enter_dispatch(self):
        if self.dispatch_ctx is None:
            self.dispatch_ctx = QuantMode(self)
        return self.dispatch_ctx

class QuantMode(TorchDispatchMode):
    def __init__(self, manager: QuantManager = None):
        super().__init__()
        self.mgr = manager

    def __torch_dispatch__(self, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
        args = [self.mgr.model.quantizer(a) if isinstance(a, torch.Tensor) and a.dtype == torch.float32 else a for a in args]
        kwargs = {k: self.mgr.model.quantizer(v) if isinstance(v, torch.Tensor) and v.dtype == torch.float32 else v for k, v in (kwargs or {}).items()}
        return func(*args, **kwargs)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = ToyModel(hidden=8, num_blocks=2)
    a = torch.randn(2, 8, dtype=torch.float32)
    b = torch.randn(2, 8, dtype=torch.float32)

    manager = QuantManager(model)
    with manager.enter_dispatch():
        with torch.no_grad():
            exported_program = torch.onnx.export(manager.model, (a, b), dynamo=True)

Feature request:
Add a lightweight progress bar utility (based on tqdm) in torch.utils that users can optionally import to visualize training/validation/test loop progress.
Motivation:
PyTorch core currently does not provide any built-in progress tracking for long-running loops. While users can integrate tqdm manually, it requires repetitive boilerplate in tutorials and quick scripts. A small utility in torch.utils would lower the barrier for beginners and improve user experience without adding significant complexity to the core library.
Pitch:
The utility would remain optional, minimal, and import tqdm only if used. This way, PyTorch maintains its philosophy of flexibility while offering a small but meaningful quality-of-life improvement for users.
Alternatives
No response
Additional context
No response

Use machine with B200 GPUs and cuda 12.8
Install torch nightly build for cuda 12.8: pip3 install --pre torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu128
Clone torchao git clone git@github.com:pytorch/ao.git

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=7 python cast_bench.py --mode dim0_mxfp8_floor

nodes.bodyText:
grad_outputs is type hinted as Optional[_TensorOrTensors], and _TensorOrTensors is defined as _TensorOrTensors: TypeAlias = Union[Tensor, Sequence[Tensor]].
However the documentation says:

None values can be specified for scalar Tensors or ones that don't require grad.

I don't think it's possible to have any output that doesn't require grad (so this sentence may also need to be updated, if I understand correctly), but it's perfectly possible to have scalar outputs, and providing a None grad_output for each of them works just fine.
So I think the type hint should rather be Optional[_TensorOrOptionalTensors], with _TensorOrOptionalTensors defined as _TensorOrOptionalTensors: TypeAlias = Union[Tensor, Sequence[Optional[Tensor]]]
This also applies to a few other places:

The grad_tensors parameter of torch.autograd.backward
The (deprecated) grad_variables parameter of torch.autograd.backward
The grad_outputs parameter of torch.autograd.gradgradcheck
The tensors parameter of _tensor_or_tensors_to_tuple (a helper function in torch/autograd/__init__.py that is only used on grad_outputs or grad_tensors).)

What do you think? I can try to make a PR for this if you agree.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
I was asked recently to investigate allowing use of FSDP2 with cuda graph in pytorch.
I discovered several issues:

torch.chunk_cat, which is used in FSDP2, allocates pinned host memory. That is currently unsafe in cuda graph capture, but I have a fix to this that I will upload shortly.
make_graphed_callables does not support running with models with any hooks. It says you can add hooks to a torch.nn.Module after having called make_graphed_callables on it, but this is clumsy because you need the hooks to all-gather all of your weights in order to warmup. Warmup is the only safe way to guarantee a  workload can be captured to a cuda graph today. If you could somehow add the hooks for the sake of warmup, remove the hooks for the sake of make_graphed_callables, and then re-add the hooks, I suppose you could warmup successfully. However, make_graphed_callables is an old API that came out when cuda graphs were first added to pytorch. I personally do not think that the requirement that a module not have hooks is overly cautious. We don't need it. I am investigating making a new variant of make_graphed_callables that drops this requirement.
At least once, a stream fails to join against the capturing stream during stream capture: 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/fsdp/_fully_shard/_fsdp_collectives.py
    
    
         Line 247
      in
      1981ed4
    
  
  
    

        
          
           with device_handle.stream(all_gather_copy_in_stream): 
        
    
  

 This means this work is not recorded inside the cuda graph, causing a mismatch between graph replay and eager execution.

Unfortunately, several workloads using FSDP2 can become host latency bounded, so cuda graph support is something reasonable to want for it.
I can take care of these issues myself, but I wanted to document them so that people are aware. I also don't personally know the FSDP2 maintainers, so I wanted to make sure they were aware as well.
Alternatives
No response
Additional context
No response

🐛 Describe the bug
If the optimizer is provided parameters which are not used as part of the loss function calculation, they do not get an internal optimization state (e.g. a state used by in Adam). This confuses the torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict.set_state_dict function and it errors. The error happens even if StateDictOptions(strict=False) and DefaultLoadPlanner(allow_partial_load=True) is used.
import pathlib
import shutil

import torch
import torch.optim as optim
import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp
from torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict import get_state_dict, set_state_dict, StateDictOptions
from torch.distributed.checkpoint.stateful import Stateful
from torch.distributed.checkpoint import DefaultLoadPlanner

class AppState(Stateful):
    def __init__(self, model, optimizer):
        self.model = model
        self.optimizer = optimizer

    def state_dict(self):
        # this line automatically manages FSDP FQN's, as well as sets the default state dict type to FSDP.SHARDED_STATE_DICT
        model_state_dict, optimizer_state_dict = get_state_dict(self.model, self.optimizer)
        return {
            "model": model_state_dict,
            "optim": optimizer_state_dict
        }

    def load_state_dict(self, state_dict):
        # sets our state dicts on the model and optimizer, now that we've loaded
        set_state_dict(
            self.model,
            self.optimizer,
            model_state_dict=state_dict["model"],
            optim_state_dict=state_dict["optim"],
            options=StateDictOptions(strict=False)
        )

tmp_dir = pathlib.Path("test/tmp/test_dataset_datamodule_resume")
shutil.rmtree(tmp_dir, ignore_errors=True)

# Model + optimizer
model = torch.nn.Linear(4, 2, bias=True)
optimizer = optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)

# One training step
loss = torch.mean(model.weight)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

# Save checkpoint
dcp.save({'app': AppState(model, optimizer)}, checkpoint_id=tmp_dir)

# Recreate model + optimizer and load
model2 = torch.nn.Linear(4, 2, bias=True)
optimizer2 = optim.AdamW(model2.parameters(), lr=0.01)

# RuntimeError: Missing key in checkpoint state_dict: optimizer.state.bias.step.

🐛 Describe the bug
We notice the ExportedProgram partitioner may change input order.
For example, for inputs in origin EP sent to Partitioner is [input_ids, attention_mask].
However, the EP sent to backend preprocess become [attention_mask, input_ids].
After analysis, the root cause comes from one function in the torch side.
The workflow for partition is below:

Executorch partitioner gives each node a tag, meaning they can be grouped into a partition.
The ExecuTorch partitioner will call torch fuse_as_graphmodule to fuse nodes with same tag.
fuse_as_graphmodule will follow the visit order from nodes passed, to create the new placeholder in new graph.
Since the passed in nodes first use attention_mask, the input order of ExportedProgram in graph become [attention_mask, input_ids]


https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/2507ae63f293354170695fd20a5c5ce5f64e323d/torch/fx/passes/utils/fuser_utils.py

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
When splitting a simple model that contains an nn.Embedding layer into pipeline stages with the torch.distributed.pipelining.pipeline API, the pipeline representation incorrectly calls the embedding layer twice.  The second call passes the embedding output (a FloatTensor) as the index argument to nn.Embedding, but nn.Embedding expects an index tensor of type LongTensor.  During execution, the compiled graph inserts an aten._assert_tensor_metadata.default node that checks the dtype of the tensor, and this assertion fails with a Tensor dtype mismatch! Expected: Float, Got: long long error.
To reproduce

Using PyTorch 2.8.0 (tested on Python 3.11, macOS 13.5, CPU), create the following repro.py:

import torch
from torch.distributed.pipelining import pipeline, SplitPoint

class X(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, hidden_states):
        return hidden_states.to(torch.float32)

class Y(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.embed_tokens = torch.nn.Embedding(32, 16, -1)
        self.layers = torch.nn.ModuleList([X() for _ in range(2)])

    def forward(self, input_ids):
        x = self.embed_tokens(input_ids)
        _dummy_tensor = torch.zeros(2, 1, 32, 32)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return x

def main():
    model = Y()
    # split before the second layer
    split_point = "layers.1"
    example_input_ids = torch.randint(0, 32, (2, 32), dtype=torch.long)
    print("--- Splitting model into pipeline stages ---")
    try:
        pipe = pipeline(
            model,
            mb_args=(example_input_ids,),
            split_spec={split_point: SplitPoint.BEGINNING},
        )
        print("\n--- Running pipeline ---")
        _output = pipe(example_input_ids)
        print("\n--- Execution successful (bug not reproduced) ---")
    except Exception as e:
        print("\n--- ERROR (bug reproduced) ---")
        print(f"Error message: {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run the script: python repro.py.

Expected behavior
The pipeline created by pipeline(model, …) should behave like the original model: the micro‑batch of integer token indices is embedded to floats, passes through two trivial X modules that call .to(torch.float32), and returns a FloatTensor.  No dtype mismatch should occur.
Observed behavior
Instead of running successfully, the pipeline throws an error:
--- Splitting model into pipeline stages ---
--- Running pipeline ---
--- ERROR (bug reproduced) ---
Error message: Tensor dtype mismatch! Expected: Float, Got: long long

While executing %_assert_tensor_metadata_default : [num_users=0] = call_function[target=torch.ops.aten._assert_tensor_metadata.default](args = (%embedding_default,), kwargs = {dtype: torch.float32, device: cpu, layout: torch.strided})
…
GraphModule:
    def forward(self, input_ids: "i64[2, 32][32, 1]"):
        …
        embed_tokens: "f32[2, 32, 16]" = self.embed_tokens(input_ids, embed_tokens_weight_1)
        …
        embed_tokens_1 = self.embed_tokens(embed_tokens)  # incorrect second call
        …

The compiled graph has created a submodule submod_0.embed_tokens whose forward() simply asserts that its input has dtype torch.float32 and returns an empty list.  However, the graph erroneously calls self.embed_tokens a second time with the embedding output as its argument.  Because nn.Embedding expects its first argument to be a tensor of integer indices (LongTensor), this second call leads to a mismatch between the expected and actual dtypes.  The assertion inserted by torch.export fails and raises the error shown above.
Analysis
•	According to the pipeline parallelism documentation, the pipeline API traces the model with torch.export and splits it into submodules around the specified split_spec.  It should preserve the original forward behavior and activation flow across splits.
•	The reproduction model is full‑graphable and does not perform any dynamic control flow.
•	When inspecting the generated graph (shown in the error message), the pipeline inserted two calls to embed_tokens: the first call correctly consumes the LongTensor input IDs and produces a FloatTensor embedding; the second call mistakenly consumes the FloatTensor embedding.  This is not present in the original model.
•	Because nn.Embedding expects integer indices as input, passing a FloatTensor triggers the dtype assertion in the exported graph.  If the _dummy_tensor = torch.zeros(…) line is removed, the error does not reproduce.

Additional context
•	The error occurs even when torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float32) is set; the issue is not related to default dtype.
•	Changing the split point to layers.0 or using SplitPoint.END produces similar errors.
•	On PyTorch 2.7.1, the same script runs without errors, suggesting this regression was introduced in 2.8.0.

Versions
•	PyTorch version: 2.8.0 (installed via pip)
•	Python version: 3.11
•	OS: macOS (both Intel and Apple Silicon)
•	Device: CPU
•	Repro script is single‑process (no distributed processes).

🐛 Describe the bug
When using torch.distributed.checkpoint.save_async in a setup with only one rank async_save breaks. As far as I can see there is no indication in the documentation that this should not work and torch.distributed.checkpoint.save works fine. Additionally, asynchronous checkpoint is quite useful in single-rank setups.
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp
from torch.distributed.checkpoint.stateful import Stateful

class AppState(Stateful):
    def __init__(self, value: int = 0):
        self.value = value

    def state_dict(self):
        return {
            "value": self.value,
        }

    def load_state_dict(self, state):
        self.value = state['value']

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if not dist.is_initialized():
        dist.init_process_group(
            backend="gloo",
            rank=0,
            world_size=1,
            init_method="file:///tmp/tmpfile"
        )

    app_state = AppState(value=7)
    state = {"app": app_state}
    future = dcp.async_save(state, checkpoint_id="checkpoints/ckpt")
    future.result() # AttributeError: 'FileSystemReader' object has no attribute 'storage_meta'

    restored = AppState()
    state = {"app": restored}
    dcp.load(state, checkpoint_id="checkpoints/ckpt")

    assert restored.value == app_state.value

🐛 Describe the bug
Similar to #156062 (cannot reproduce now, may be fixed), torch.nn.functional.conv_transpose3d returns all nan when the weight contains inf on MPS.
import torch
input = torch.zeros((1, 1, 5, 5, 5), dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.zeros((1, 1, 3, 3, 3), dtype=torch.float32)
weight[0, 0, 0, 0, 0] = float('inf')

input_mps = input.to("mps")
weight_mps = weight.to("mps")
out_mps = torch.nn.functional.conv_transpose3d(input=input_mps, weight=weight_mps)
out_cpu = torch.nn.functional.conv_transpose3d(input=input, weight=weight)
print(out_cpu) # contains zero
print("--------------------------------")
print(out_mps.cpu()) # all nan
Versions
nightly built
cc @kulinseth @malfet @DenisVieriu97 @jhavukainen
nodes.title: [MPS] `torch.nn.functional.conv_transpose3d` return unexpected results when weight containing `inf`

import torch
from torch.utils._python_dispatch import TorchDispatchMode

class MyTorchDispatchMode(TorchDispatchMode):
    @classmethod
    def is_infra_mode(cls):
        return True
    
    def __torch_dispatch__(self, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
        kwargs = {} if kwargs is None else kwargs
        out = func(*args, **kwargs)
        return out

def fn(x):
    return x + 2

torch._dynamo.config.recompile_limit = 1
torch.compiler.reset()
fn_compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", dynamic=True, fullgraph=True)

for bs in [2, 4, 8, 16]:
    x = torch.randn(bs, 4)
    with (
        MyTorchDispatchMode(),  # no errors if I remove this context
        torch.no_grad(),
    ):
        out = fn_compiled(x)

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
When using the score mode in Flexattention, the create mask function returns a boolean tensor. At the same time, when using the mask mode, it returns a float tensor. I believe these two might be reversed. The mask tensor should be a float tensor when using score mode, and it should be a boolean tensor when using mask mode.
# torch/nn/attention/flex_attention.py
# create_mask
    with TransformGetItemToIndex():
        if mod_type == _ModificationType.SCORE_MOD:
            score_mod = mod_fn
            score_mod = _vmap_for_bhqkv(score_mod, prefix=(0,))  # first input is score
            out = score_mod(torch.zeros(B, H, Q_LEN, KV_LEN, device=device), b, h, m, n)
            mask = torch.where(torch.isneginf(out), False, True)
            return mask
        elif mod_type == _ModificationType.MASK_MOD:
            mask_mod = mod_fn
            mask_mod = _vmap_for_bhqkv(mask_mod, prefix=())
            mask = mask_mod(b, h, m, n)
            return mask
        else:
            raise AssertionError

a=torch.tensor([1,2,3,4,5]).to("xpu")

test1=(a == b).cpu().sum()

a=torch.tensor([1,2,3,4,5]).to("xpu")
b=torch.tensor([3,2,4,5,5]).to("xpu")

test1=(a == b).cpu().float()
print(test1)

test2=(a == b).float().cpu()

Actually, if the tensor is already in XPU, then there is no way to change the tensor dtype, such as tensor.type

🐛 Describe the bug
import torch
import sys
torch._dynamo.config.capture_scalar_outputs = True
torch._dynamo.config.capture_dynamic_output_shape_ops = True
torch._inductor.config.emulate_precision_casts = True

def foo(arg0, arg1, arg2):
    t0 = arg0 # size=(16, 38073, 1), stride=(38073, 1, 1), dtype=float32, device=cuda
    t1 = t0.clone(); t1.zero_() # size=(16, 38073, 1), stride=(38073, 1, 1), dtype=float32, device=cuda
    t2 = t1.contiguous().view((49, 112, 111)) # size=(49, 112, 111), stride=(5488, 112, 1), dtype=float32, device=cuda
    t3 = arg1 # size=(1,), stride=(1,), dtype=int64, device=cuda
    t4 = arg2 # size=(1,), stride=(1,), dtype=int64, device=cuda
    t5 = t3 + t3 + t4 # size=(1,), stride=(1,), dtype=int64, device=cuda
    t6 = torch.exp(t5) # size=(1,), stride=(1,), dtype=int64, device=cuda
    t7 = torch.nn.functional.layer_norm(t2, (111,)) # size=(49, 112, 111), stride=(12432, 111, 1), dtype=float32, device=cuda
    output = t7  # output tensor
    return output

🐛 Describe the bug
There are a few rough edges in .ci/docker/requirements-docs.txt (which docs/requirements.txt is a symlink of):

pip install -r docs/requirements.txt pulls numpy 2.x, which is incompatible with the pinned versions of matplotlib and tensorboard.
The pinned matplotlib versions mean it's only possible to install these requirements on Python 3.9/3.10:

matplotlib==3.5.3 ; python_version < "3.13"
matplotlib==3.6.3 ; python_version >= "3.13"

because matplotlib 3.5.3 only supports Python <=3.10, and matplotlib 3.6.3 only supports Python <=3.11.
I imagine there are some historical constraints I may not be aware of.

If we can't upgrade the pinned matplotlib and tensorboard versions, we should at least pin numpy<2 and make sure the library versions we're pinning are compatible with the Python versions they're pinned for.
If we can upgrade matplotlib and tensorboard, we'd ideally upgrade to versions which support numpy>2, obviating the issue and possibly enabling the use of a single environment for development and building the docs.

Perhaps this should be a separate issue, but we should also update the dependencies in tools/nightly.py. At a glance, it's missing expecttest (causes errors while running tests). It includes sphinx, which makes me think it's intended to work for building the docs - but if that's true, it's missing other dependencies it'd need like matplotlib.
Also see #163789 - opening this as a separate issue as per @janeyx99's suggestion.
python3.10 -m venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
python -c "import matplotlib.pyplot"  # fails with ImportError

This is to discuss if we want to automatically register the autograd fallback for PrivateUse1 all the time or not.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Repro
import torch.symm_mem._nvshmem_triton as nvshmem

@triton.jit
def foo(...):
    nvshmem.get(...)

def run():
    nvshmem.enable_triton()
    foo[(1, )]()

Cause
The previous enable_triton UI requires the user-defined Triton kernel have a "nvshmem" in its name. But this requirement is in the doc and sometimes the user does not notice it.
If users did not do so, the kernel would miss the NVSHMEM init, and silently hit CUDA IMA.
Versions
main
cc @H-Huang @awgu @wanchaol @fegin @fduwjj @wz337 @wconstab @d4l3k @pragupta @ezyang @msaroufim @dcci
